l261.title: The staff and the bass clef
l261.objective: Recognize the staff, the bass clef and the note F.
l261.s1: “Tab tells you where to play. The staff tells you what sounds and for how long.”
l261.s2: Five lines and four spaces, counted from the bottom up. Higher on the staff means a higher note.
l261.s3: “Is this clef an ear? No: it's the bass clef. Its two dots hug the F line.”
l261.s4: At the start of every line of music, the bass clef marks the fourth line: that's F.
l261.c1b: The staff has 5 lines and 4 spaces, counted from the bottom up. The higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. Listen to this scale climb.
l261.c2b: The clef starts on the 4th line, and its two dots sit just above and below that line. That line is F: every other note is counted from it.
l261.c3b: The bass sounds an octave lower than written, so its notes fit comfortably on the staff. That's why your open E string sits on a ledger line, below the five lines.
l261.q1: Which line does the bass clef mark?
l261.q1o1: The 4th line, counting from the bottom
l261.q1h: Look for the line between the two dots.
l261.q2: Which note sits on the clef's line?
l261.q2h: It's the note that gives the clef its other name: the F clef.
l261.q3: One note sits higher on the staff than another. How does it sound?
l261.play: Play the clef's F: D string, fret 3. Two half notes and a whole note.

l262.title: Open strings on the staff
l262.objective: Read the 4 open strings on the staff.
l262.s1: “You already know your 4 open strings. Now you'll see them on the staff.”
l262.s2: E sits on the ledger line below; A, in the first space.
l262.s3: “D on the middle line, G in the top space. Like climbing stairs!”
l262.s4: The spaces spell A, C, E, G; the lines spell G, B, D, F, A.
l262.c1b: E, the lowest string, sits on a ledger line below the staff. A is right above it, in the first space.
l262.c2b: D is on the middle line, the third one. G, the highest string, is in the fourth space, at the top.
l262.c3b: In bass clef, the spaces from the bottom up are A, C, E, G: All Cows Eat Grass. The lines are G, B, D, F, A: Good Boys Do Fine Always. Listen: spaces first, then lines.
l262.q1: Which open string is this note?
l262.q1h: Check whether it's on a line or in a space, and which one.
l262.q3h: It's outside the staff, on a ledger line.
l262.read: Read the staff and tap each open string on the fretboard.
l262.play: Now with your bass: the 4 open strings, up and down, in half notes.

l263.title: Note values and rests on the staff
l263.objective: Read whole, half, quarter and eighth notes and their rests.
l263.s1: “In tab you saw the rhythm underneath. On the staff, the shape of the note tells you how long it lasts.”
l263.s2: Whole: hollow. Half: hollow with a stem. Quarter: filled. Eighth: filled, with a flag or a beam.
l263.s3: “A rest isn't nap time: you count it too. Shh… two, three, four.”
l263.s4: Stems point up on low notes and down from the middle line.
l263.c1b: Whole note: 4 beats, hollow, no stem. Half note: 2 beats, hollow with a stem. Quarter note: 1 beat, filled. Eighth note: half a beat; two eighths together share a beam. Listen to one bar of each.
l263.c2b: Each note value has a rest of the same length. The whole rest hangs from the 4th line; the half rest sits on the 3rd. During a rest, mute the string and keep counting.
l263.c3b: Low notes have the stem going up, on the right. From the middle line up, it goes down, on the left. It doesn't change the sound: it just makes the music easier to read.
l263.q1: How many beats does each of these notes last?
l263.q1h: Hollow with a stem: it's a half note.
l263.q2: How many notes sound in this bar?
l263.q3: What are notes joined by a beam?
l263.q3o1: Eighth notes: half a beat each
l263.play: Play with the metronome: a whole note, two half notes, two quarters and a half on A, then four quarters on E.

l264.title: E- and A-string notes on the staff
l264.objective: Read and write the natural notes on the E and A strings, plus the sharp.
l264.s1: “On the E string you already know F and G. Where are they written? Climbing, one by one.”
l264.s2: E, F, G: ledger line, the space below the staff, the first line. Each natural note climbs one step.
l264.s3: “A hashtag next to F? No: it's a sharp. It raises the note a half step, one fret.”
l264.s4: Writing is the same thing backwards: hear the note, find its step and draw it.
l264.c1b: On the E string: open E goes on the ledger line; F (fret 1) in the space below the staff; G (fret 3) on the first line.
l264.c2b: On the A string: open A in the first space; B (fret 2) on the 2nd line; C (fret 3) in the 2nd space; D (fret 5) on the middle line.
l264.c3b: A ♯ before a note raises it a half step: one fret. F on the E string is fret 1; F♯ is fret 2. It's written in the same spot as F, with the ♯ in front.
l264.c4b: D at fret 5 on the A string and the open D string are the same note: they're written the same way. The staff tells you what sounds; you choose where to play it.
l264.q3: Listen and write the names: which three notes did you hear?
l264.q3h: The first one is the lowest of all: the open E string.
l264.read: Read the melody on the staff and tap each note on the fretboard.
l264.play: Now with your bass: the same melody, at 66 bpm.

l265.title: Reading a piece: the Canon
l265.objective: Read and play Pachelbel's Canon bass line from the staff.
l265.s1: “This line is over 300 years old and still plays at weddings. And it's a bass line.”
l265.s2: Pachelbel wrote it around 1680: 8 notes that repeat while the violins change on top.
l265.s3: “I read F and played F… but it had a sharp. Look at the whole note before you play it!”
l265.s4: Before you play, check the clef, the tempo and the sharps. Then always read one note ahead.
l265.c1b: Johann Pachelbel wrote his Canon around 1680. The bass repeats 8 notes over and over while the violins keep changing on top: it's the foundation that holds everything up. Listen.
l265.c2b: Check the clef, the tempo, how many bars there are and whether any ♯ shows up. Here there's one: F♯, at fret 2 on the E string.
l265.c3b: While you play one note, your eyes are already on the next. Half notes give you time: two beats to get your hand ready.
l265.q1: Which note in this line has a sharp?
l265.q1h: Look for the ♯ in front of a note.
l265.q2: A bass line that repeats the same pattern through a whole piece is called…
l265.read: Read the Canon bass line on the staff and tap each note on the fretboard.
l265.play: Now with your bass: the Canon twice in a row, in half notes.

l111.title: Meet your bass
l111.objective: Name 9 parts of the bass and identify the 4 strings by name and by sound.
l111.s1: “The bass ties the drums' rhythm to the chords. Without bass, the band floats.”
l111.s2: Headstock and tuning pegs, neck, frets and markers, body, pickups, bridge, volume and tone knobs, and the cable jack.
l111.s3: From thickest to thinnest: {{e}}, {{a}}, {{d}} and {{g}}. The thickest goes on top, nearest your face.
l111.s4: “The thickest string sounds the lowest. Low is on top, high is at the bottom.”
l111.c1b: Tuning pegs, a neck with frets, a body with pickups and bridge, the knobs and the cable jack.
l111.c2b: 4th E, 3rd A, 2nd D and 1st G. They're numbered from thinnest to thickest.
l111.c3b: The thicker the string, the lower its sound. That's why open E is the lowest note on the bass.
l111.ear: Listen. Which open string is it?
l111.play: Play the open string that lights up.

l112.title: Posture
l112.objective: Hold the bass sitting and standing, with the strap at the right height and the neck angled slightly up.
l112.s1: “If your bass slips or your back hurts, it's not your fault: it's your posture.”
l112.s2: Sitting: the bass body rests on the leg on your plucking-hand side, back straight. The neck points slightly up.
l112.s3: “Strap down at your knees? Very rock and roll, but your wrists will suffer.”
l112.s4: Standing, the bass sits at the same height as when you're sitting. That way you practice one position.
l112.c1b: Armless chair, feet flat. The bass body rests on the leg on your plucking-hand side; the neck points slightly up.
l112.c2b: Adjust the strap so the bass sits at the same height as when you're sitting.
l112.c3b: Loose shoulders, straight wrists. If something hurts, stop, shake out your hands and check your posture.
l112.q1: Which way does the neck point?
l112.q2: How high do you set the strap?
l112.q2h: You practice one position, sitting or standing.
l112.play: Sit up straight and play each open string when it lights up.

l113.title: The amp
l113.objective: Plug your bass into an amp (or a headphone amp) and set volume and tone without noise.
l113.s1: “An electric bass barely makes a sound on its own. It needs an amp.”
l113.s2: First, the amp volume at zero. Plug in the cable, then turn it up little by little.
l113.s3: “Plug in with everything at full… BOOM! Now the neighbors know you've started playing.”
l113.s4: Volume at zero, plug in, turn it up slowly. The tone knob makes the sound rounder or brighter.
l113.c1b: Amp volume at zero, cable from bass to amp, and only then switch on and turn up.
l113.c2b: Start with the bass knobs all the way up and set the level on the amp. Loud enough to hear clearly, but not too loud.
l113.c3b: Turning tone down makes the sound rounder and darker; turning it up, brighter. Start in the middle.
l113.q1: What do you do before plugging in the cable?
l113.q1o1: Turn the amp volume down to zero
l113.q1o2: Turn everything up to test it
l113.q1o3: Tune the bass with the cable in my hand
l113.q1h: That way you avoid the pop when you plug in.
l113.q2: You want a rounder, darker sound. Which knob do you use?
l113.q2o1: Turn the tone down a little
l113.play: Play open E and open G, one after the other. Set the volume so you hear both clearly.

l114.title: Tuning to E-A-D-G
l114.objective: Tune all 4 strings with the tuner and check them by ear.
l114.s1: “Strings drift out of tune with weather and use. That's why you tune before every practice.”
l114.s2: The tuner has a needle and a circle that turns green when the note is right on.
l114.s3: “If the note goes up, you're on track. If you overshoot, go down a bit and come back up.”
l114.s4: Trick: fret 5 on one string sounds the same as the next open string.
l114.c1b: Green: in tune (±5 cents). Left: too low, tune up. Right: too high, tune down.
l114.c2b: Turn it a little at a time. The direction depends on the bass: watch whether the needle goes up or down.
l114.c3b: Fret 5 on E = open A. Fret 5 on A = D. Fret 5 on D = G.
l114.ear: Listen to both sounds. Is the second one higher or lower?
l114.tune: Tune each string until the circle turns green.

l115.title: Your starting routine
l115.objective: Tune on your own and recognize the 4 open strings by ear.
l115.s1: “Every practice starts the same way: tune up and say hi to all four strings.”
l115.s2: Tune E, A, D and G with the tuner. Then play them from lowest to highest and back.
l115.s3: “A string sounds off? Don't keep going: tune it again. It takes ten seconds.”
l115.s4: Tuning and listening to the open strings: two minutes that set up your whole practice.
l115.c1b: One string at a time, until the tuner turns green. Always before you play.
l115.c2b: E is the lowest and G the highest. With practice you'll know them without looking.
l115.tune: Tune all 4 strings: E, A, D and G.
l115.ear: First you hear open E, then another open string. Which is the second one?
l115.route: Play the open strings from E to G and back to E.

l121.title: Alternate plucking
l121.objective: Pluck alternating index and middle fingers (i-m) with a steady pulse at 60 bpm.
l121.s1: “Your fingers walk just like your feet: one, then the other.”
l121.s2: Your thumb rests on the pickup. The finger pulls the string toward the body and comes to rest on the next string.
l121.s3: Two mistakes: always using the same finger, and pulling the string outward.
l121.s4: “One note per click. i, m, i, m.”
l121.c1b: Index (i) in blue, middle (m) in orange. The thumb rests on the pickup.
l121.c2b: Repeating one finger tires you out. Pulling the string outward makes it snap.
l121.walk: Finger walk: alternate i and m with the metronome.
l121.playE: Open E string in quarter notes, alternating i and m.
l121.playEA: One bar on E and one on A, alternating.

l122.title: Your thumb
l122.objective: Rest your thumb on the pickup or on the E string, depending on the string you play.
l122.s1: “My thumb doesn't play, but it works hard.”
l122.s2: Playing E: thumb on the pickup. Playing A, D or G: the thumb moves down and rests on the E string.
l122.s3: “Thumb in the air = a floating hand and buzzing strings.”
l122.s4: Your thumb always rests somewhere: on the pickup or on the E string.
l122.c1b: For the E string, on the pickup. For A, D and G, on the E string.
l122.c2b: Resting on E, your thumb steadies your hand and keeps that string from ringing on its own.
l122.q: You're about to play the D string. Where does your thumb rest?
l122.qh: Only the E string gets the thumb on the pickup.
l122.walk: A slightly faster finger walk: alternate i and m.
l122.play: Eight quarter notes on D and eight on G, with your thumb resting on the E string.

l123.title: Crossing strings
l123.objective: Move from one string to another without losing the i-m alternation or the beat.
l123.s1: “Changing strings is like climbing a step without looking at your feet.”
l123.s2: Keep alternating i and m. Whichever finger plays after the change goes straight to the new string.
l123.s3: “The same finger twice in a row to change strings? Tempting, but no.”
l123.s4: Always alternate, even when you change strings.
l123.c1b: i, m, i, m without a break, even when you change strings. Don't repeat a finger.
l123.c2b: When you cross, your hand barely moves: your fingers reach the new string from where they are, and each one still comes to rest on the next string.
l123.q: You played E with i. The next note is on the A string. Which finger?
l123.EA: E and A in turn, then A and D. One note per click.
l123.ladder: The ladder: from E to G and back, twice.

l124.title: Muting strings
l124.objective: Keep strings you're not playing from ringing, using your plucking hand.
l124.s1: “A string that nobody plays but keeps ringing is like a guest who won't leave.”
l124.s2: Your thumb and the finger that just played mute the thicker strings. Thinner ones, a free finger resting on them.
l124.s3: “You play G, then E… and G keeps ringing. Mute it!”
l124.s4: Only the string you play should sound.
l124.c1b: Your thumb mutes the E string, and the finger that just played comes to rest on the next thicker string.
l124.c2b: When you go back to a thicker string, rest a free finger of your plucking hand on the thin string you played before.
l124.q1: You play the A string. What mutes the E string?
l124.q2: You played G and now you play E. What happens to G?
l124.q2o1: It stops right away on its own
l124.q2o2: It keeps ringing unless you mute it
l124.q2h: An open string rings until something touches it.
l124.play: Four quarter notes on G, four on E, four on D and four on A. Mute the previous string at each change.

l125.title: Alternating on open strings
l125.objective: Go across the 4 open strings alternating i and m, at 70 bpm or faster, with no extra strings ringing.
l125.s1: “Today we put it all together: thumb, alternating, changing strings and muting.”
l125.s2: Four quarter notes per string, from E to G and back, always i-m.
l125.s3: “If a string keeps ringing, don't stop: mute it on the next pass.”
l125.s4: With this, your plucking hand is ready. Now it's the other hand's turn, the one that presses the frets!
l125.c1b: Resting thumb, i-m alternation, crossing strings and muting the previous string.
l125.c2b: If it gets messy at 70 bpm, practice at 60. Speed comes on its own once the motion is clean.
l125.route: Four quarter notes on each string, from E to G and back to E.

l131.title: One finger per fret
l131.objective: Fret with fingers 1 to 4 on frets 1 to 4 and play “the spider” on one string.
l131.s1: Your thumb sits behind the neck, level with your middle finger. Fingers curved, as if holding a ball.
l131.s2: “Press with your fingertip, nice and curved, like a little hammer.”
l131.s3: Finger 1 on fret 1, finger 2 on fret 2, and so on up to 4: one finger per fret.
l131.s4: “If your hand hurts, stop and shake it out. Playing shouldn't hurt.”
l131.c1b: Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (pinky). The thumb has no number.
l131.c3b: On the E string, frets 1 to 4 are F, F♯, G and G♯.
l131.fb: Tap frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the E string, in order.
l131.hint: Count the frets from the nut.
l131.spiderE: The spider on the E string: 1-2-3-4 in quarter notes.

l132.title: The sweet spot
l132.objective: Press right behind the fret so the note rings clean, with as little pressure as possible.
l132.s1: “Hear that buzz? That's my finger, far from the fret.”
l132.s2: Press right behind the fret. There the string rests on the metal and the note rings clear.
l132.s3: “Squeeze like you're juicing a lemon and you'll get tired. A light touch is enough.”
l132.s4: Close to the fret, curved finger, light pressure: a clean note.
l132.c1b: Right behind the fret, on the nut side. Not on top of the fret and not in the middle of the space.
l132.c2b: Start light and press a little harder until the buzz goes away. That's all the pressure you need.
l132.c3b: Move your finger closer to the fret and press with the fingertip, finger curved. Check that no other finger touches the string.
l132.q1: Where does the note ring cleanest?
l132.q1o2: In the middle of the space
l132.q1h: Think of scene 2 of the cartoon.
l132.q2: The note buzzes. What do you try first?
l132.q2o2: Press as hard as I can
l132.fb: Tap frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the A string, in order.
l132.play: On the A string, each fret twice: 1-1-2-2-3-3-4-4. Make every note ring clean.

l133.title: The spider walks back
l133.objective: Play the spider going down (4-3-2-1) with your fingers already in place.
l133.s1: “The spider walks backwards too. Without tripping!”
l133.s2: Rest all four fingers on frets 1 to 4. Play and lift 4, then 3, then 2, then 1.
l133.s3: “Lift your whole hand at once and the spider falls. One finger at a time.”
l133.s4: Going down, the next finger is already in place: you just lift the one in front.
l133.c1b: To go down from 4 to 1, start with all four fingers in place. For each note, lift one finger and play.
l133.c2b: While your fingers walk, your thumb stays put behind the neck.
l133.fb: Tap the spider going down: frets 4, 3, 2 and 1 on the E string.
l133.q: You go from fret 4 down to 3. What does your fretting hand do?
l133.down: The spider going down on the E string: 4-3-2-1 in quarter notes.
l133.updown: Up and down on the E string: 1-2-3-4-4-3-2-1.

l134.title: Changing strings
l134.objective: Move the spider from one string to the next without breaking the beat.
l134.s1: “I made it to fret 4… now what? On to the next string!”
l134.s2: After finger 4 on the E string, finger 1 goes to fret 1 on the A string, right on time.
l134.s3: “Stop to look for the fret and the band keeps going without you.”
l134.s4: Get the next finger ready while the note rings: that way the beat never breaks.
l134.c1b: From fret 4 on one string to fret 1 on the next: finger 1 travels while 4 is still ringing.
l134.c2b: The finger that plucks moves to the new string and you keep alternating i and m.
l134.q: You played fret 4 on the E string. Where does finger 1 go?
l134.qo1: To fret 1 on the A string
l134.qo2: To fret 5 on the E string
l134.qo3: To fret 1 on the G string
l134.qh: The spider climbs string by string: E, A, D and G.
l134.fb: Tap the spider on the E string and keep going on the A string: 1-2-3-4, 1-2-3-4.
l134.EA: The spider on E and A, twice, without breaking the beat.
l134.DG: The spider on D and G, twice, without breaking the beat.

l135.title: The full spider
l135.objective: Play the spider across all 4 strings, up and down, at 70 bpm.
l135.s1: “Today the spider walks across all four strings. Will you join me?”
l135.s2: Climb from E to G with 1-2-3-4. Come down from G to E with 4-3-2-1.
l135.s3: “If you make a mistake, don't start over: keep the beat going.”
l135.s4: The spider is your everyday warm-up: two minutes before you play.
l135.c1b: Up: 1-2-3-4 on E, A, D and G. Down: 4-3-2-1 on G, D, A and E.
l135.c2b: A mistake doesn't stop the music. Keep the beat and fix it on the next note.
l135.ear: Listen: first open E, then a note on frets 1 to 4. Which one is it?
l135.fb: Tap the spider going down: frets 4, 3, 2 and 1 on the G string, then on the D string.
l135.full: The full spider: climb across all 4 strings and come back down.

l141.title: Reading tab
l141.objective: Read from the tab which string and fret to play.
l141.s1: “This isn't scary sheet music: it's your 4 strings, drawn.”
l141.s2: In tab, the bottom line is the E string, the thickest one. The top line is the G string.
l141.s3: “Does 3 mean finger 3? No: it means fret 3. And 0 is the open string!”
l141.s4: Line = string. Number = fret. Read it from left to right.
l141.c1b: Each line is a string. From bottom to top: E, A, D and G.
l141.c2b: The number tells you which fret to press. 0 means open string.
l141.c3b: Read it from left to right, like text. The vertical lines split the line into bars: more on those soon.
l141.q1: In tab, which string is the bottom line?
l141.q1h: It's upside down from how you see your bass while playing.
l141.q2: You see a 2 on the second line from the bottom. What do you play?
l141.tab: Read the tab and tap each note on the fretboard.
l141.play: Now on your bass: the same tab, one note per click.

l142.title: The beat
l142.objective: Keep a steady beat with the metronome and hold it when the click goes quiet.
l142.s1: “Feel that thing that makes your foot tap? That's the beat.”
l142.s2: The metronome marks the beat with a click. We count beats in groups of 4: 1, 2, 3, 4.
l142.s3: “If the click goes quiet, don't rush: the beat keeps going.”
l142.s4: Bass and drums look after the beat for the whole band.
l142.c1b: It's the steady heartbeat of the music. You mark it with your foot or your head.
l142.c2b: We group beats in fours and count 1, 2, 3, 4. On the metronome, 1 sounds louder.
l142.q: How many beats do you count in each bar in these lessons?
l142.click: Tap the beat with the metronome for 4 bars.
l142.alone: Now the click stops halfway. Keep tapping the beat.
l142.play: Four beats on each open string: E, A, D and G.

l143.title: Whole, half and quarter notes
l143.objective: Recognize whole, half and quarter notes and play them for their full length.
l143.s1: “Some notes go by fast, and others stay a while.”
l143.s2: A quarter note lasts 1 beat, a half note 2 and a whole note 4: it fills the whole bar.
l143.s3: “A half note isn't a quarter note in a hurry: let it ring for two beats.”
l143.s4: Quarter 1, half 2, whole 4. Count while it rings.
l143.c1b: Filled head and a stem. It lasts 1 beat.
l143.c2b: Hollow head with a stem. It lasts 2 beats.
l143.c3b: Hollow head, no stem. It lasts 4 beats: a whole bar.
l143.q1: How many beats does a half note last?
l143.q2: Which note fills a 4-beat bar on its own?
l143.tab: Tap each note and listen to how long it lasts.
l143.play: A whole note, two half notes, four quarter notes and another whole note. Let each one ring.

l144.title: Counting out loud
l144.objective: Count 1, 2, 3, 4 out loud while you play mixed note values.
l144.s1: “I count out loud. That's not for beginners: that's what pros do.”
l144.s2: Say “1, 2, 3, 4” with the metronome. Every note starts on one of those numbers.
l144.s3: “If you get lost, wait for the next 1 and come back in.”
l144.s4: Counting out loud tells you where every note sits in the bar.
l144.c1b: A half note on 1 rings through 1 and 2; the next note starts on 3.
l144.c2b: If you get lost, don't stop: wait for 1 of the next bar and carry on.
l144.q: A bar has a half note, a quarter note and a quarter note. On which number does the second quarter note start?
l144.qh: The half note takes up 1 and 2.
l144.tempo: Count out loud and tap the beat. The click stops after 2 bars.
l144.tab: Read the tab while counting every beat out loud.
l144.play: Play the line counting out loud: half notes, quarter notes and a whole note at the end.

l145.title: Steady beat
l145.objective: Hold the beat for 24 beats without a metronome and play a 4-bar line read from tab.
l145.s1: “Today the metronome takes a break. Can you keep the beat?”
l145.s2: First 8 beats with the click, then 24 without it. Count in your head.
l145.s3: “If you rush, no big deal: breathe and get back on the beat.”
l145.s4: With a steady beat and tab, you're ready to read your first bass lines.
l145.c1b: Count in your head and tap your foot. The metronome is a help, not a crutch.
l145.c2b: While you play one bar, look at the next one.
l145.pulse: 8 beats with the click and 24 without. Keep the beat.
l145.tab: Read the 4-bar line on the fretboard.
l145.play: Play the line on your bass, counting all 4 bars.

l151.title: The root
l151.objective: Know what a chord's root is and play it in quarter notes.
l151.s1: “Guitar and keys play chords. I play their most important note: the root.”
l151.s2: The root is the note a chord is named after. E chord: root E. A chord: root A.
l151.s3: “If I play some other note, the guitarist gives me a funny look.”
l151.s4: Four quarter-note roots per bar: that's the sound of thousands of songs.
l151.c1b: It's the note the chord is named after. When the band plays an A chord, the bass plays A.
l151.c2b: Four quarter notes of the same note in each bar: the simplest line, and one of the most used.
l151.q: The band plays an A chord. Which note do you play?
l151.qh: The root has the same name as the chord.
l151.tab: Read the E and A roots on the tab.
l151.play: Roots in quarter notes: one bar of E, one of A, twice.

l152.title: I, IV and V
l152.objective: Find the roots of the I, IV and V chords in the key of E.
l152.s1: “Loads of songs use just three chords. Three!”
l152.s2: In the key of E, those chords are E, A and B. Roots: open E, open A and A string fret 2.
l152.s3: “They're called I, IV and V for their place in the scale. Don't worry: scales come later.”
l152.s4: I, IV and V: three roots close together, to play your first songs.
l152.c1b: In the key of E: I = E, IV = A, V = B.
l152.c2b: E: open E string. A: open A string. B: A string, fret 2, with finger 2.
l152.q: In the key of E, where do you play the root of V (B)?
l152.tab: One whole note per chord: I, IV, V and back to I.
l152.play: I–IV–V–I in the key of E: one bar of quarter notes per chord.

l153.title: Changing on time
l153.objective: Move from one root to the next right on beat 1 of the bar.
l153.s2: On beat 4, get your hand ready for the next root. On 1, you're already there.
l153.s3: “Get there late and the band changes chords without you.”
l153.c1b: While beat 4 rings, your finger is already traveling to the next root.
l153.c2b: While you play one bar, read the root of the next one.
l153.q: On which beat do you get ready to change to the next root?
l153.quarters: I–IV–V–I in quarter notes at 80 bpm. Change right on 1.
l153.halves: Now in half notes: two roots per bar. Get ready on 2 and on 4.

l154.title: A new key: A
l154.objective: Play I–IV–V in the key of A, with roots on open strings.
l154.s1: “Let's change key: now home is A.”
l154.s2: In the key of A, the roots of I, IV and V are A, D and E: three open strings!
l154.s3: “The E string sounds lower than the A, but it's still the V. Surprise!”
l154.s4: Same numbers, I–IV–V; different key, different roots.
l154.c1b: I = A, IV = D, V = E. All three are open strings.
l154.c2b: The root can be lower or higher: what matters is that it's the chord's note.
l154.q: In the key of A, what's the root of IV?
l154.tab: Read I–IV–V–I in the key of A.
l154.play: I–IV–V–I in the key of A, in half notes, with a whole note at the end.

l155.title: Kordi Groove 1
l155.objective: Play an 8-bar line over I–IV–V with mixed note values, at 70 bpm or faster.
l155.s1: “This is my first groove. Now it's yours too.”
l155.s2: Each bar: a half note and two quarter notes on the root. E, A, B and back to E.
l155.s3: “Bar 4 has a surprise: two quarter notes and the half note at the end.”
l155.s4: You finished level 1! You can play a complete bass line.
l155.c1b: Bars 1 to 4: E, A, B, E. Bars 5 to 8: the same, ending with a whole note on E.
l155.c2b: Half, quarter, quarter: count “1-2, 3, 4”. In bar 4 it flips: “1, 2, 3-4”.
l155.q: Which root do you play in bar 3?
l155.qh: The groove goes through I, IV, V and I.
l155.tab: Read the first 4 bars of the groove.

cp1.intro: Show what you learned in level 1: ear, tab, beat, the spider and Kordi Groove 1 at 80 bpm.
cp1.ear: First you hear open E, then another open string. Which is the second one?
cp1.tab: Read the 4-bar tab and tap each note on the fretboard.
cp1.pulse: 80 bpm: 8 beats with the click and 24 without.
cp1.spider: The full spider: climb across all 4 strings and come back down.
cp1.groove: The full Kordi Groove 1 at 80 bpm.

checkpoint.2: Checkpoint 2 · Strummed chords and a palm-muted riff
checkpoint.3: Checkpoint 3 · Short solo with bends and vibrato
checkpoint.4: Final project · Your solo over a backing track

goal.1_3: Play the 1-2-3-4 chromatic on all 6 strings, one finger per fret.
goal.1_4: Mute the strings you are not playing with both hands.
goal.1_5: Read chord diagrams and tab with quarter notes, eighth notes and rests.

goal.2_2: Add C, G, D and Dm.
goal.2_3: Switch chords while strumming quarter and eighth notes without losing the pulse.
goal.2_4: Move the fifth shape with the root on the 6th and 5th strings to play riffs.
goal.2_5: Mute with your palm on the bridge to give riffs weight.
goal.2_6: Play the minor pentatonic in 1st position with a metronome.

goal.3_2: Slide between notes landing on the right fret.
goal.3_3: Bend a half step and a whole step right in tune.
goal.3_5: Play barre chords rooted on the 6th string all over the neck.
goal.3_6: Play barre chords rooted on the 5th string.
goal.3_7: Find every natural note on the 6th and 5th strings.
goal.4_2: Connect the boxes and move horizontally.
goal.4_3: Build them by intervals and play them in two positions.
goal.4_4: Use Dorian, Mixolydian and Phrygian from the major scale.

goal.4_6: Raise your alternate-picking tempo while staying clean.

l111.title: Meet your electric guitar
l111.objective: Name 9 parts of the electric guitar and identify the 6 strings by number and by sound.
l111.s1: "Hi! I'm Kordi. Today I swapped my bass for an electric guitar. Let's get to know it together."
l111.s2: Tuning pegs, nut, neck with frets, body, pickups, selector, volume and tone knobs, bridge and output jack.
l111.s3: Six strings, from thickest to thinnest: E, A, D, G, B and E. Listen to them climb.
l111.s4: "There are two Es: the 6th, thick and low, and the 1st, thin and high. They are two octaves apart."
l111.c1t: The parts of the electric guitar
l111.c1b: Look at the drawing and find each number on your guitar. The pickups are magnets that "listen" to the strings and send the signal to the amp.
l111.c2b: They are numbered from the thinnest: 1st E, 2nd B, 3rd G, 4th D, 5th A and 6th E. The 6th is on top, closest to your face.
l111.c3b: The thicker the string, the lower the sound. Listen to the 6th and the 1st: both are E, but two octaves apart.
l111.q2: Which part turns the strings' vibration into the signal that goes to the amp?
l111.ear: You'll hear both E strings. Which one is the high one?
l111.play: With the amp on, play the open string that lights up, from the 6th to the 1st.

l112.title: Plug guitar into amp
l112.objective: Plug the guitar into the amp in the safe order and get it sounding at a comfortable volume.
l112.s1: "An unplugged electric guitar barely makes a sound. Its voice lives in the amp."
l112.s2: First, amp volume at 0. Then plug the cable into the guitar and the amp. Only then turn it on.
l112.s3: The amp has knobs: GAIN, BASS, MIDDLE, TREBLE and VOLUME. Today you only use VOLUME.
l112.s4: "Turn the volume up slowly while you play the 6th string, until it sounds clear but not deafening."
l112.c1b: 1: the cable goes into the guitar's jack. 2: the other end goes into the amp's INPUT. 3: with the volume at 0, turn the amp on and bring it up slowly. That way you avoid a loud pop in the speaker and in your ears.
l112.c2b: GAIN adds drive, BASS the lows, MIDDLE the mids, TREBLE the highs and VOLUME the overall level.
l112.c3t: The app hears you through the amp
l112.c3b: For the exercises with your guitar, keep the phone near the amp. Without an amp, the microphone barely picks up an electric guitar. If you use a multi-effects unit or a headphone amp, connect it to a speaker.
l112.q1: What do you do before plugging in the cable?
l112.q1o1: Turn the amp volume all the way up
l112.q1o3: Turn the amp volume down to 0
l112.q2: Which amp knob controls how loud everything is?
l112.play: With the amp at a comfortable volume, play the open 6th string 4 times.

l113.title: Tune all 6 strings
l113.objective: Tune the 6 strings with the app's tuner to within 5 cents.
l113.s1: "An out-of-tune guitar sounds bad even if you play perfectly. Tuning always comes first."
l113.s2: Play a string and watch the needle. Left means the string is flat: tighten the peg. Right means it's sharp: loosen it.
l113.s3: Tune from the 6th to the 1st: E, A, D, G, B, E. Listen to how it should sound.
l113.s4: "Turn a little and play again. When the needle sits in the middle, in teal, you're in tune."
l113.c1b: Needle in the middle and teal: in tune. If it's on the left, raise the string (tighten). If it's on the right, lower it (loosen). It's best to reach the note from below.
l113.c2b: From the 6th to the 1st: E, A, D, G, B, E. Play the example to hear the 6 strings in tune.
l113.c3b: The 5th fret of a string sounds the same as the next open string. There is one exception: on the 3rd string (G), the 4th fret gives you the 2nd string (B).
l113.ear: Listen to two notes. Is the second one higher or lower?
l113.tune: Tune each string that lights up until the needle sits in the middle.

l114.title: Pickups, volume and tone
l114.objective: Choose a pickup with the selector and use the guitar's volume and tone knobs.
l114.s1: "My guitar has three pickups. Each one hears the string in a different spot."
l114.s2: The neck pickup sounds round and warm. Listen.
l114.s3: The bridge pickup sounds bright, with more bite. Hear the difference.
l114.s4: "The guitar's knobs change volume and tone before the signal reaches the amp."
l114.c1b: Pickup 1 is the neck, 2 the middle, 3 the bridge. A 5-way selector picks one or blends two neighbors. Many guitars have 2 pickups and a 3-way selector: same idea.
l114.c2b: Round, warm sound. Great for soft melodies and blues solos.
l114.c3b: Bright sound with bite. The favorite for rock riffs and for crunch.
l114.c4b: 1: guitar volume. 2 and 3: tone; at 10 it keeps all the brightness, and turning it down makes it darker. To practice, leave everything at 10 and control volume on the amp.
l114.ear: Listen. Which pickup is it: neck or bridge?
l114.q1: You want a bright sound with lots of bite for a riff. Which pickup do you choose?
l114.play: Try the pickups: play the strings that light up, first on the neck pickup and then on the bridge.

l115.title: Your clean sound
l115.objective: Set the amp for a clean sound and tell clean from crunch by ear.
l115.s1: "Now let's build your sound. Every amp knob at halfway, and GAIN low."
l115.s2: With GAIN at 2 the sound is clean: every note comes through clearly. That's how we practice most of the time.
l115.s3: With GAIN at 6 you get crunch: the sound gets a little dirty and gains punch. Listen.
l115.s4: "Crunch is for some riffs. For learning, and so the app hears you well, go back to clean."
l115.c1b: Start with BASS, MIDDLE and TREBLE at 5. If it sounds dull, raise TREBLE. If it sounds thin, raise BASS. MIDDLE gives it body so the guitar cuts through the band.
l115.c2b: 1: GAIN low, at 2 or 3. 2: VOLUME to taste. It's the sound for practicing and the one the app hears best.
l115.c3b: 1: GAIN at 6, just slightly driven. 2: lower VOLUME a bit, because crunch sounds louder. You'll use it for power chords and palm muting.
l115.ear: Listen. Is the sound clean or crunchy?
l115.play: With a clean sound, play the 6 open strings from the 6th to the 1st and back.

l121.title: Posture
l121.objective: Sit with the guitar in a comfortable posture and play the 6th string to a steady pulse.
l121.s1: "Good posture lets you play longer without getting tired or hurt."
l121.s2: Back straight, against the chair. The guitar on your leg, with the neck pointing slightly up.
l121.s3: Shoulders relaxed. Your picking arm rests on the guitar body; the other elbow stays close to your body.
l121.s4: "Let's try: one note per click, on the 6th string."
l121.c1b: 1: back straight. 2: the guitar resting on your leg. 3: the neck slightly up, never toward the floor. 4: both feet on the ground. If you play standing, adjust the strap so the guitar sits at the same height.
l121.c2b: If your shoulders creep up or your wrist bends sharply, stop, breathe and settle back in. Practicing through pain doesn't help.
l121.q1: When sitting, where does the guitar rest?
l121.q1o2: On your leg, with the neck slightly up
l121.q1o3: With the neck pointing at the floor
l121.pulse: Keep the pulse with the metronome: one tap per click.
l121.play: Play the open 6th string, once per click.

l122.title: Hold the pick
l122.objective: Hold the pick between thumb and index finger and play downstrokes to a steady pulse.
l122.s1: "The pick is the electric guitar's tool. Small, but it's the boss."
l122.s2: Curl your index finger. Rest the pick on the side of its last joint and close it with your thumb, flat.
l122.s3: Let just the tip show. Strike downward from the wrist, not from the elbow.
l122.s4: "If the pick spins or drops, grip a little tighter. Just a little."
l122.c1b: 1: thumb flat on top. 2: index finger curled underneath. 3: the tip shows, about 2 or 3 mm. If too much shows, the pick catches on the string.
l122.c2b: 1: the pick moving toward the floor. 2: this table-shaped sign means "downstroke" in sheet music.
l122.c3b: The motion is short and comes from the wrist, as if shaking off a drop of water. The arm barely moves.
l122.q1: How much of the pick tip should show?
l122.q2: To start, which part of the pick touches the string?
l122.play: Downstrokes on the 4th string (D), once per click.

l123.title: Downstrokes on every string
l123.objective: Move from string to string with downstrokes without losing the pulse.
l123.s1: "You can play one string. Now let's travel across all six."
l123.s2: To change strings, move your whole hand, not just the pick. The motion stays short.
l123.s3: Four times on each string, from the 6th to the 1st. Listen.
l123.s4: "If you hit the wrong string, slow down. Accurate first, fast later."
l123.c1b: 1: the hand travels from the 6th to the 1st. 2: the pick stays the same distance from the string. Look at the next string, not the one you're playing.
l123.c2b: Play the example: four quarter notes per string, with the metronome. That's how the exercise sounds.
l123.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l123.play: Four times on each string, from the 6th to the 1st, with downstrokes.

l124.title: Alternate picking
l124.objective: Alternate down and up strokes in eighth notes at 60 bpm without losing the pulse.
l124.s1: "Down, up, down, up. That way the pick plays twice as much without working twice as hard."
l124.s2: On the click, down. Between clicks, up. Those are eighth notes: two notes per beat.
l124.s3: The table sign means down; the V means up. They always alternate, even when you change strings.
l124.s4: "If you mix them up, say it out loud: 'down', 'up'. It works."
l124.c1b: 1: downstroke, on the beat. 2: upstroke, between beats. The upward motion is as short as the downward one.
l124.c2t: This is how eighth notes sound
l124.c2b: Sixteen eighth notes on the 3rd string (G), with a click on every beat. Play the example and count: "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and".
l124.c3b: Alternate picking never stops: even if a note is missing, the hand keeps going up and down. That way you don't lose time.
l124.tap: Tap ↓ and ↑ in turn: two taps per click.
l124.play: Eighth notes on the 3rd string (G): down on the click, up between clicks.

l125.title: Your first riff
l125.objective: Play a 4-bar riff on open strings at 60 bpm or faster.
l125.s1: "Listen to this! It's a riff made only of open strings. Today you play it."
l125.s2: It jumps between the 6th, 5th, 4th and 3rd strings. Look closely at the tab before you play.
l125.s3: Now clean and slower, with the metronome. That's how you'll practice it.
l125.s4: "When you nail it at 60, move up to 70 and 80. Then try it with crunch."
l125.c1b: Four bars on open strings. Play the example and follow the tab: the 0s mean open string.
l125.c2b: 1: the pick jumps from one string to another without lifting much. 2: look at the next string before you play it.
l125.c3b: This is how it sounds with a bit of GAIN. Practice it clean; once you've got it, try crunch just for fun.
l125.tab: Read the riff in the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l125.play: Play the whole riff with the metronome.

l131.title: One finger per fret
l131.objective: Fret frets 1 to 4 on the 6th string with one finger per fret, with no buzzing.
l131.s1: "So far you've used open strings. Today your other hand joins the show."
l131.s2: Index on fret 1, middle on 2, ring on 3 and pinky on 4. Your thumb goes behind the neck.
l131.s3: Press right behind the fret, with your fingertip. Listen: frets 1, 2, 3 and 4.
l131.s4: "If the note buzzes, move your finger closer to the fret. You don't need to press harder."
l131.c1b: 1: index. 2: middle. 3: ring. 4: pinky. 5: your thumb, resting behind the neck, roughly behind finger 2. The thumb has no fretting number.
l131.c2b: Each finger takes care of one fret, so your hand doesn't jump around. Play the example: frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the 6th string.
l131.c3b: Press with your fingertip, right next to the fret (on the nut side). That way the note rings clean with little effort.
l131.tap: Tap frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 of the 6th string on the fretboard.
l131.play: Fret and play frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 on the 6th string, twice.

l132.title: Chromatic on the 6th and 5th
l132.objective: Play the 1-2-3-4 chromatic up and back on the 6th and 5th strings at 60 bpm or faster.
l132.s1: "This exercise has a name: the chromatic. Guitarists warm up with it every day."
l132.s2: Frets 1-2-3-4 on the 6th, then on the 5th, and back: 4-3-2-1. Listen.
l132.s3: One finger per fret. When you move to the 5th string, your hand stays put: only your fingers change strings.
l132.s4: "Keep your fingers close to the strings. Far away, they waste time."
l132.c1b: Go up 1-2-3-4 on the 6th and 5th, then down 4-3-2-1 on the 5th and 6th. Play the example and follow the tab.
l132.c2b: When you lift a finger, let it hover near the string. That way it gets to the next note on time.
l132.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l132.play: Chromatic up and back on the 6th and 5th strings, with the metronome.

l133.title: Chromatic on the 4th and 3rd
l133.objective: Play the 1-2-3-4 chromatic up and back on the 4th and 3rd strings at 60 bpm or faster.
l133.s1: "The middle strings: D and G. Same exercise, new spot."
l133.s2: Frets 1-2-3-4 on the 4th, then on the 3rd, and back. Listen.
l133.s3: To reach the 3rd string, your wrist drops a little. Your thumb stays behind the neck.
l133.s4: "Pinky getting tired? That's normal. It gets stronger after a few days of practice."
l133.c1b: The same chromatic on the 4th (D) and 3rd (G). Play the example and follow the tab.
l133.c2b: Finger 4 is the weakest. Don't swap it for finger 3: that's exactly what this exercise trains.
l133.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l133.play: Chromatic up and back on the 4th and 3rd strings, with the metronome.

l134.title: Chromatic on the 2nd and 1st
l134.objective: Play the 1-2-3-4 chromatic up and back on the 2nd and 1st strings at 60 bpm or faster.
l134.s1: "The thin strings sound high and need less pressure."
l134.s2: Frets 1-2-3-4 on the 2nd, then on the 1st, and back. Listen.
l134.s3: On thin strings, press lightly: if you squeeze too hard, the note goes sharp.
l134.s4: "Make sure your finger doesn't touch the next string. Press with the tip, standing upright."
l134.c1b: The chromatic on the 2nd (B) and 1st (E). Play the example and follow the tab.
l134.c2b: Thin strings go out of tune if you press too hard. Press just enough for a clean note.
l134.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l134.play: Chromatic up and back on the 2nd and 1st strings, with the metronome.

l135.title: All 6 strings, up and back
l135.objective: Play the chromatic on all 6 strings, up and down, at 60 bpm or faster.
l135.s1: "Listen: all six strings, end to end. This is the full exercise."
l135.s2: Go up 1-2-3-4 from the 6th to the 1st, and down 4-3-2-1 from the 1st to the 6th.
l135.s3: That's 48 notes. If you get lost, keep the pulse and pick it up on the next string.
l135.s4: "Once you've got it at 60, move to 70 and 80. That's your daily warm-up."
l135.c1b: Four notes per string, up to the 1st and back down to the 6th. Play the example and follow the tab.
l135.c2b: A few minutes of chromatic before practicing wakes up your fingers and your alternate picking.
l135.pulse: Keep the pulse: the click stops after 8 beats and you carry on.
l135.play: The chromatic on all 6 strings, up and back, with the metronome.

l141.title: Muting with the fretting hand
l141.objective: Stop a fretted note by relaxing your finger, without lifting it off the string.
l141.s1: "Listen to this note. It keeps ringing, and ringing… What if I want it to stop?"
l141.s2: Relax your finger but keep it resting on the string. The note stops instantly.
l141.s3: Note and rest, note and rest. Listen.
l141.s4: "If you lift your finger all the way, the open string rings. Relaxing isn't letting go."
l141.c1b: 1: the finger stays on the string, without pressing. 2: the string stops ringing. If you lift it off, the open string sounds: that's noise.
l141.c2b: Each note lasts one beat and the next beat is a rest. Play the example: the note stops right on the click.
l141.ear: Listen. Does the note ring long or is it cut short?
l141.play: Note and rest: play on the click and mute by relaxing your finger on the next click.

l142.title: Muting with the picking hand
l142.objective: Stop an open string by resting your picking hand on it, in time.
l142.s1: "An open string has no finger to relax. How do you stop it?"
l142.s2: Rest the edge of your palm on the string, near the bridge. Done: silence.
l142.s3: Play, rest, play, rest. Listen to how each note stops.
l142.s4: "Both hands mute. With practice they do it on their own, without thinking."
l142.c1b: 1: the edge of your picking hand rests on the strings, near the bridge. 2: the strings it touches stop ringing.
l142.c2b: Open string on the click and a rest on the next click. Play the example and listen for the cut.
l142.q1: You played the open 6th string and want it to stop. What do you do?
l142.q1o1: Rest the edge of my picking hand on the string
l142.q1o2: Press harder with the other hand
l142.play: Open string and rest: mute with your picking hand on every rest.

l143.title: Rests in the rhythm
l143.objective: Respect the rests in a rhythm: nothing rings where there's no note.
l143.s1: "In music, you play the silence too."
l143.s2: Listen: notes and rests mixed together. During a rest, the pulse keeps going.
l143.s3: On the rhythm line under the tab, a rest has its own sign.
l143.s4: "Count the rests out loud. That way you won't skip them."
l143.c1b: Under the tab, where there's no number, you see the rest sign: the quarter rest looks like a zigzag and lasts 1 beat; the half rest is a small block and lasts 2.
l143.c2b: During a rest, no string should ring. Mute with whichever hand you need.
l143.pulse: Keep the pulse, during the rests too.
l143.play: Play the rhythm with its rests, with the metronome.

l144.title: Noise-free riff
l144.objective: Play a riff with fretted notes, open strings and rests, with no extra strings ringing.
l144.s1: "Listen to this crunchy riff. Notice that nothing rings between the notes."
l144.s2: Fretted notes are muted by relaxing your finger.
l144.s3: Open strings are muted with your picking hand.
l144.s4: "Now clean and slow. Noise-free first, faster later."
l144.c1b: Four bars with notes on the 6th and 5th strings and rests. Play the example and follow the tab.
l144.c2b: With gain, any string left ringing really stands out. That's why muting matters so much on electric guitar.
l144.play: Play the riff with the metronome, muting on every rest.

l151.title: 6-line tab
l151.objective: Read which string and fret to play on all 6 strings from tab.
l151.s1: "Tab is the fastest way to write music for guitar."
l151.s2: Six lines, one per string. The 1st (high E) is on top; the 6th (low E) is at the bottom.
l151.s3: The number tells you the fret: 0 is an open string. Listen and follow the tab.
l151.s4: "Careful: the top line is the highest string, even though it's at the bottom of your guitar."
l151.c1b: In tab, the top line is the 1st string (the thinnest) and the bottom one is the 6th (the thickest). It's like looking down at the neck.
l151.c2b: Each number is a fret. 0 = open. Read left to right. Play the example and follow the numbers.
l151.q1: In tab, which string is the top line?
l151.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.

l152.title: Note lengths in tab
l152.objective: Read quarter, half and whole notes in tab and play them for their full length.
l152.s1: "Tab tells you where to play. The note shapes underneath tell you how long."
l152.s3: The shapes sit under each number. Listen to this line and count.
l152.s4: "Don't rush a half note: let it ring for two full beats."
l152.c1b: The quarter note (filled head with a stem) lasts 1 beat; the half note (hollow with a stem), 2; the whole note (hollow, no stem), 4. Play the example and count 1, 2, 3, 4.
l152.c2b: Four bars mixing all three. Play the example and follow the shapes under the tab.
l152.q1: How many beats does a half note last?
l152.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l152.play: Play the line, holding each note for its full length.

l153.title: Eighth notes and rests
l153.objective: Read and play eighth notes and rests in tab, with alternate picking.
l153.s1: "Eighth notes are the quick ones: two per beat."
l153.s2: In tab, the eighth note has a little flag on its stem. Play it with alternate picking: down, up.
l153.s3: Listen: eighth notes, quarter notes and rests in the same bar.
l153.s4: "Count '1 and 2 and'. Eighth notes land on the number and on the 'and'."
l153.c1b: It lasts half a beat: two eighth notes fill one beat. Under the tab they have a little flag. Play the example and count "1 and 2 and".
l153.c2b: Four bars with eighth notes, quarter notes and rests. Alternate picking keeps going even during rests.
l153.tap: Tap ↓ and ↑ in turn: two taps per click.
l153.play: Play the line with eighth notes and rests, using alternate picking.

l154.title: Chord diagrams
l154.objective: Read a chord diagram: strings, frets, fingers and which strings ring.
l154.s1: "Before playing chords, let's learn to read their picture: the diagram."
l154.s2: It's the neck standing up: vertical strings, horizontal frets and the nut on top.
l154.s3: This is E minor (Em): finger 2 on the 5th string and finger 3 on the 4th, both on fret 2. Listen.
l154.s4: "An X means 'this string doesn't ring'. An O means 'it rings open'. Look at this A minor."
l154.c1b: 1: vertical strings, the 6th on the left. 2: horizontal frets. 3: the nut, the thick line on top. 4: the dot shows where to press and the number which finger. 5: O is open; X, don't play it.
l154.c2b: Fingers 2 and 3 on fret 2 of the 5th and 4th strings; the other four open. Listen to it string by string.
l154.c3b: The 6th string has an X: don't play it. You'll play chords in level 2; today you just read them.
l154.q1: In a chord diagram, what are the vertical lines?
l154.q2: What does an X above a string mean?
l154.tap: Tap the two fretted notes of E minor on the fretboard: fret 2 on the 5th and 4th strings.

l155.title: Sight-reading
l155.objective: Read and play a new 4-bar tab without hearing it first.
l155.s1: "Today's challenge: reading a tab you've never heard."
l155.s2: First look at the whole tab: which strings and frets it uses.
l155.s3: Then count the rhythm without playing, and only then play it, slowly.
l155.s4: "This is how it sounds once you've got it. With crunch!"
l155.c1b: 1: look at strings and frets. 2: count the rhythm out loud. 3: play it slowly with the metronome. Reading well matters more than playing fast.
l155.c2b: Do the reading exercise first. If you get stuck, play the example and follow the tab.
l155.tab: Read the new tab and play each note on the fretboard.
l155.play: Play the whole tab with the metronome.

cp1.ear: The first note is the open 6th string. Which open string comes next?
cp1.tab: Read the tab and play each note on the fretboard.
cp1.pulse: Keep the pulse at 80 bpm: the click stops after 8 beats and you carry on.
cp1.spider: The chromatic on all 6 strings, up and back, at 70 bpm.
